title: The Man Who Lost His Axe
text:
A man in ancient China lost his axe and could not find it anywhere. He began to suspect his neighbor's son.

Once the thought had come to him, he watched the boy closely. The way the boy walked looked like the walk of a man who had stolen an axe. His expression looked like the expression of a man who had stolen an axe. The way he spoke sounded exactly like the way a thief speaks. Everything the boy did, every gesture and every look, seemed to show that he was the one who had taken it.

Some time later the man was digging in his own garden, or in some versions clearing a ditch in his own valley, and his spade struck metal. It was his axe, lying where he himself had dropped it.

The next day he saw the neighbor's son again. Now nothing about the boy's walk, his face or his manner looked in the least like a thief.
lesson: Once you suspect someone, you start reading every small sign as proof. Check the facts before you let a suspicion color how you see a person.
date: c. 4th century BC to 4th century AD
source: Liezi, Chapter 8 (Shuo Fu); a version also in the Lushi Chunqiu
caveat: The dating of the Liezi is disputed; parts of it may have been compiled as late as the 4th century AD.
